boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Lynchburg record (June 17-18, 1864) in the Lynchburg Campaign [May-June 1864]. The June 17 fight at Diamond Hill (Quaker church) is inside the frozen interval and part of this record. Duffie's raid, the Lexington delay, the pursuit through Liberty on June 19 and the loss of guns near Salem on June 21 are context. Campaign marches, the destruction at Staunton and Lexington, the retreat to the Kanawha and campaign-wide loss and capture totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force text is 'Corps (44,000 total)' and the battle-level strength field 44000; the side rows are blank and the live page gives zero totals. Hunter says Crook and Averell joined him at Staunton on June 8 with about 10,000 men and two batteries, and that he had thirty guns at Lexington; Pond gives Averell 4,400, the joined column about 10,000, and Hunter about 18,000 with thirty guns. Hunter sent back 800 men with a convoy from Staunton and a regiment with the wagon train on the 16th. For the defenders, Hunter reports rumors ranging from a few thousand invalids and militia to all the West Virginia forces under Breckinridge plus Ewell's corps of 20,000; on the 17th the force was 'variously estimated at from 10,000 to 15,000'; on the 18th prisoners told him Early's whole corps, 20,000 strong, was at or near Lynchburg, and he judged the enemy at least double his strength. Pond says half of Early's corps reached the city on the 17th; Early says only the part of his command that was up repulsed the attack on the 18th.
claims.rationale: Hunter's and Pond's figures are for June 8 at Staunton, before detachments; the Confederate figures are rumors, estimates and prisoners' statements. The frozen 44,000 is not traced to any inspected passage. None is adopted as a matched opening strength; live zeros are not measured absence.

claims.value: Hunter says Averell found the enemy strongly posted and intrenched at Diamond Hill, five miles from Lynchburg, on the 17th, and that the city's works were strong redoubts on each main road about three miles apart, flanked by rifle-pits protected by abatis, which the defenders were extending during the 18th. Pond calls the first position Quaker church, five miles out, says the enemy was shut up in a redoubt two miles from the city, and describes redoubts protected by abatis; the Union attacked along the Bedford turnpike, the Forest road and the Campbell road.
claims.rationale: The city works were occupied before Hunter arrived (Pond says Breckinridge placed troops behind them) and were being extended during the action; their construction date is not established, so the claim is not tagged inherited. Diamond Hill and Quaker church may name the same position. No map verification.

claims.value: Hunter says that by the afternoon of the 18th his troops had scarcely enough ammunition for another well-contested battle; he had waited a day at Lexington for a 200-wagon supply train and sent it back from beyond Liberty on the 16th. Pond says he no longer had ammunition for a pitched battle against Early, his rations were nearly gone and he was 200 miles from his base. NPS says he withdrew because of a critical shortage of supplies. On the Confederate side, Pond says the Charlottesville railroad, already repaired, brought Early's troops forward.
claims.rationale: Commander's and historian's statements, not ammunition or ration returns.

claims.value: Hunter says neither his scouts nor other sources gave clear or reliable information about the enemy, so he advanced to develop the truth; through the night of the 17th trains ran without intermission and cheering and drums suggested arriving troops, but until the morning of the 18th he had no positive information whether Lee had detached a considerable force; prisoners taken on the 18th said part of Ewell's corps was engaged. Pond says Breckinridge at Lynchburg had scanty information of Hunter's progress, and that Hunter's delay at Lexington was enough to prove the salvation of Lynchburg.
claims.rationale: Hunter's account of what he knew is his August report; Pond's judgments are retrospective.

claims.value: The frozen commanders are Major General David Hunter (US) and Lieutenant General Jubal A. Early (CS); the live page gives Early as Major General. Hunter reconnoitered the lines, ordered Duffie to attack on the Forestville road while Averell sent cavalry against the Campbell Court-House road, and ordered the trains away and the night withdrawal. Pond says Breckinridge had placed his and Vaughn's troops behind the works long before Hunter arrived, with home guards and convalescents and Generals D. H. Hill and Hays aiding, and that Early put two brigades of Ramseur's division into the redoubt on the 17th. Hunter attributes the sortie of the 18th to Breckinridge ('the bloody repulse of Breckinridge'), while Early calls it an assault on his lines repulsed by his command.
claims.rationale: Breckinridge, not a listed commander, directed the defense before and possibly during part of the action; who directed the Confederate troops on the 18th is disputed. The live rank is not adopted. No listed commander receives automatic credit.

claims.value: The frozen and live results are Confederate victory. On the 17th Hunter's advance carried the works at Diamond Hill (Quaker church), taking 70 prisoners and a gun. On the 18th Hunter says the enemy advanced from its works, was routed after an hour and twenty minutes and driven back in disorder, but that he withdrew that night against a force at least double his own. Early says the enemy assaulted and was repulsed, and that he found it retreating in confusion the next morning. Pond says Hunter attacked in force, Early's infantry sallied and was driven back, and Hunter withdrew once assured Early's corps had arrived. NPS says Hunter's first tentative attacks were thwarted by the arrival of Early's vanguard.
claims.rationale: Who attacked on the 18th, and how the fight ended, is disputed; the agreed outcome is Hunter's withdrawal. The retreat through West Virginia and its effect on Early's advance into Maryland are campaign contribution.

claims.value: The frozen total is 900; the live page gives 900 (US 700; CS 200). Pond says the Union losses were about two hundred and the Confederate must have been severe; Hunter calls his loss on the 18th comparatively light and says the enemy was driven back with heavy loss. For the whole expedition Pond quotes Strother's claim of 2,000 Confederate killed and wounded and 2,000 prisoners against a Union loss of 1,500 men and eight guns.
claims.rationale: Pond's two hundred and Hunter's 'comparatively light' cover the action of the 18th; Strother's figures are expedition-wide and are not assigned to this record. The compiled Union table for June 10-23 (No. 2, read, not selected) is garbled in OCR. No Confederate loss figure appears in the inspected passages. Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap.

open_questions: Crook's July 7 report (No. 6), Duffie's and Averell's division reports (Nos. 21-22), the brigade and regimental reports on the engagement (Nos. 7-20), McCausland's and Imboden's reports (Nos. 25-26) and the compiled Union table (No. 2, read, not selected) remain deferred. Early's June 22 dispatch (read, not selected) concerns the pursuit.
No Breckinridge report for Lynchburg was located in the inspected report list; his role rests on Pond and Hunter.

NPS/CWSAC (the live NPS page and the frozen Arnold rows) is one family. George E. Pond's The Shenandoah Valley in 1864 (Scribner, 1883) is a retrospective history written, by its preface, from the official documents at the War Records Office; in these chapters it quotes Sigel's, Hunter's, Vaughn's and Imboden's reports and despatches and Strother's report, so it is not independent of those families. Hunter's August 8 report and Early's June 19 dispatch (the targeted follow-up, for the Confederate commander's account; its year reads '1861' in OCR) printed in Official Records Series I, Volume XXXVII, Part 1, are separate families of interested commanders' accounts; the volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
